candidate.answerReason: The bottom blocks contribute with weights 1 at the three corners, 3 at the six other boundary positions, and 6 at the central position. Assigning the smallest labels to the greatest weights gives an attainable minimum of 114.

methods.label: Trace each block's contribution
methods.explanation:
A bottom number may enter the top sum several times, so we first determine how many times each position contributes. Call that number the position's weight.

Start with weight \(1\) on the top block and work downward. A block's weight is passed to each of its three supporting blocks. If several blocks pass weights to the same block, add those weights. This exactly tracks the expansion of the sums: every route from a bottom block to the top contributes one copy of its number, and each route has a unique next block above it.

The three blocks just below the top each have weight \(1\). Passing these weights down gives the following triangular arrangement on the six-block layer:
\[
\begin{array}{ccccc}
&&1&&\\
&2&&2&\\
1&&2&&1
\end{array}
\]
Passing them down once more gives the bottom weights:
\[
\begin{array}{ccccccc}
&&&1&&&\\
&&3&&3&&\\
&3&&6&&3&\\
1&&3&&3&&1
\end{array}
\]
For example, the center receives \(2+2+2=6\), each noncorner boundary position receives \(1+2=3\), and each corner receives \(1\). These account for all ten bottom positions.

To minimize the weighted sum, smaller numbers must occupy positions with larger weights. Indeed, suppose weights \(p>q\) hold labels \(x>y\). Swapping the labels decreases the sum by
\[
(px+qy)-(py+qx)=(p-q)(x-y)>0.
\]
Thus a minimum cannot contain such a pair. Put \(1\) at the center, \(2,3,4,5,6,7\) at the six positions of weight \(3\), and \(8,9,10\) at the corners. Every label is used exactly once, so this is an allowed arrangement, and the exchange argument proves that no arrangement has a smaller sum.

The smallest top number is therefore
\[
6\cdot1+3(2+3+4+5+6+7)+(8+9+10)
=6+81+27=\boxed{114},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
